models_evaluated: ten LLMs (open-access and closed-source; names not specified in text)

links.outcome: Change in LLM opioid, anxiety, stress, risk and monitoring recommendations across 34 sociodemographic variants of identical vignettes
links.effect: Marginalized groups (unhoused, Black, LGBTQIA+) often received more or stronger opioid recommendations, sometimes exceeding 90% in cancer settings, despite being labeled high risk; low-income/unemployed groups had elevated risk scores yet fewer opioid recommendations.
links.quote: Across both cancer and non-cancer cases, historically marginalized groups—especially cases labeled as individuals who are unhoused, Black, or identify as LGBTQIA+—often received more or stronger opioid recommendations, sometimes exceeding 90% in cancer settings, despite being labeled as high risk by the same models.

links.outcome: Subgroup disparities in LLM pain-management recommendations across demographic groups
links.effect: Disparities in opioid recommendations, anxiety treatment and perceived psychological stress clustered within marginalized populations even when clinical details were identical; patterns diverged from guidelines, indicating model-driven bias.
links.quote: Disparities in anxiety treatment and perceived psychological stress similarly clustered within marginalized populations, even when clinical details were identical.

unlisted_practices: Integrating guideline-based checks into LLMs for opioid prescribing recommendations

screen.reason: Empirical evaluation of 10 LLMs on acute-pain clinical vignettes to measure socio-demographic biases and disparities in opioid prescribing recommendations without testing an organizational deployment practice or guardrail.
